articles.title: NASA Awards Moon Base Transportation, Technology, Science Projects
articles.summary: NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities. The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on […]
articles.content:
Artist’s concept of living and working at Moon Base. Credit: NASA

NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities. The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon’s South Pole.

The agency shared the news at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

“We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get more better and more capable with every mission. When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”

“In the eight months since Ignition, we’ve made incredible strides in accomplishing the near impossible: establishing a permanent outpost on the lunar surface,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. “We’ve consolidated numerous efforts into a streamlined program, evolving our human exploration architecture into an iterative and sustained campaign for Moon Base technology development and implementation. Most importantly, we’ve taken action, awarding new contracts and forging new partnerships to accelerate development.”

Moon Base cargo landers

To strengthen the cargo lander network needed to support the Moon Base, NASA selected eight companies for the next phase of its CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative. The companies are eligible to compete for future lunar surface delivery missions under the new CLPS 2 contract:

Blue Origin

Firefly Aerospace

Intuitive Machines

ispace-U.S.

Lockheed Martin Space

Northrop Grumman Space Systems

SpaceX

Voyager Technologies

Under the CLPS 2 framework, the companies will provide lunar delivery services, including managing, building, and operating landers that transport NASA science, technology, and infrastructure payloads to the Moon.

The CLPS 2 framework is a 10-year, multiple-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity master contract with a combined maximum value of $10 billion. NASA increased the value of the current CLPS 1.0 contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support initial Phase One Moon Base objectives. The original CLPS contract will remain in place through November 2028, with an additional five-year period to complete awarded lunar deliveries through November 2033.

Nuclear-powered Moon rover

NASA also announced it is moving forward with development of PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration). Carrying science instruments and technology demonstrations, the six-wheeled rover will land at the Moon’s South Pole to characterize the surface and subsurface, assess resource potential, and provide data to enable landing site selection, as well as future infrastructure and exploration activities. The nuclear-powered rover can operate during long lunar nights and within permanently shadowed regions thought to harbor ice, which is crucial for a sustained human presence on the Moon.

The agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, a division of Caltech, will manage the mission and build the rover from a combination of spare flight components and engineering test models for NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers. Using proven hardware, software, and Mars rover operation approaches significantly reduces cost and enables integration and testing of the complex PROMISE rover on a shorter timeline. NASA has assessed the compatibility of the hardware with the lunar environment and determined it can tolerate the harsh conditions found near the Moon’s South Pole.

The PROMISE rover will carry a drill to extract regolith, or lunar dust, to characterize ice and other resources from approximately 3 feet (1 meter) below the surface, spectrometers for analyzing the chemical composition of surface material, temperature and radiation sensors, and visible-light cameras. It will demonstrate a next-generation, radiation-tolerant computing system, NASA’s High Performance Spaceflight Computing, and advanced autonomy sensors and algorithms. NASA is targeting late 2028 to launch PROMISE and planning an 18-month mission for the rover.

NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole. The award expands the task order awarded in May 2026 to deliver two lunar terrain vehicles to the Moon. Blue Origin will use its Mark 1 lander to deliver and deploy the rover as part of the Moon Base’s first phase.

Launch, transportation awards

Delivering Moon Base infrastructure will require a robust transportation network between Earth and the Moon. Orbital Transfer Vehicles (OTVs) act like long-distance freight trucks, carrying large loads across space. Lunar landers handle the final delivery, bringing supplies, equipment, and infrastructure safely down to the Moon’s surface.

To demonstrate those capabilities, NASA awarded six task orders as part of the agency’s Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) launch services contract. The awards were given to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin, and Impulse Space to integrate and transport Moon Base cargo.

Three mission types will allow NASA flexibility to fly science and technology demonstrations when they are ready.

The first will include missions to reduce risks of future long-term human spaceflight for lunar exploration. The missions will verify that communication and navigation methods work properly during the journey from Earth orbit to the Moon, and OTV capability to support delivery of a CLPS lunar lander to a desired orbit. This mission type will deliver the CAPSTONE 02 spacecraft to deep space to test proximity maneuvers, navigation, and communications around the Moon.

The second category of missions will prepare the lunar South Pole for human exploration by sending a group of highly mobile drones to survey the surface before astronauts arrive, enabling safer, more informed human missions while demonstrating advanced robotic capabilities. Such missions will include the agency’s MoonFall drones, designed to scout areas beyond the reach of traditional rovers, as well as delivery of additional Moon Base assets necessary to support Phase One objectives.

To reduce risk for future missions, the third mission type will test navigation technologies and demonstrate operations in multiple cislunar orbits, between Earth and the Moon. This mission type will demonstrate commercial orbital transfer capabilities intended to increase the amount of cargo that future landers can deliver to the lunar surface.

The task orders have a value of approximately $1.3 billion combined and fall under the 10-year VADR indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, which has a maximum total value of $5 billion across all contracts. The VADR contracts are managed by NASA’s Launch Services Program Office at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center as part of the agency’s Commercial Access to Space Program. By procuring multiple launch and in-space transportation services together, NASA provides industry with a more predictable set of mission opportunities while gaining access to a broader range of commercial capabilities for future lunar exploration.

Some missions will launch aboard Blue Origin’s New Glenn, Relativity Space’s Terran R, and SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rockets. In-space transportation spacecraft for these missions will be provided by Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Impulse Space, and Quantum Space.

Complementing those in-space transportation demonstrations, NASA selected SpaceX for the Cislunar Communications Deployment Demonstration under an existing lunar logistics contract. Through a Specialized Delivery Mission task order, SpaceX will launch communications satellites aboard a Starship to cislunar space in 2028. The demonstration will help inform the development of future lunar communications networks that keep astronauts, mission controllers, and the Moon Base connected.

Lunar architecture, infrastructure

To extend infrastructure capabilities on the lunar surface, NASA plans to purchase commercial components for a Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCAST), including solar arrays, batteries, and wireless power-transfer hardware. The agency awarded Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, for energy storage capability, Redwire for power generation, and Yank Technologies, Inc., for wireless power transfer in support of miniCAST.

The miniCAST will combine power and communications capabilities to support future Moon Base activities. Engineers at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, will assemble and test the systems before they are delivered to the lunar surface.

NASA expects work to begin within months, and the initial effort will involve components rather than a major integrated system. The agency also plans a separate solicitation for fully integrated power systems, which is anticipated in early 2027.

NASA intends to release a directed call under its Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships, or NextSTEP-3 B, solicitation to help close architecture-driven, high-priority data gaps for Moon Base development. The effort will help NASA gather information it needs to plan future missions, reduce risk, and support technologies and infrastructure for sustained operations on the Moon’s South Pole. The work could include small spacecraft missions, payloads on future Moon Base flights, or the purchase of data collected by commercial partners.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on this foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

To learn more about the Moon Base, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase

-end-

George Alderman / James Gannon

Headquarters, Washington

202-358-1600

george.a.alderman@nasa.gov / james.h.gannon@nasa.gov

articles.personality_title: NASA advances Moon Base plans with new rover and delivery contracts
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA is working to build a permanent base on the Moon’s South Pole. This base will help astronauts live and work on the Moon for long periods. To do this, NASA needs new technology, transportation, and science tools.

**What happened** – On Saturday, NASA announced several new contracts and projects to support the Moon Base. They chose eight companies, including SpaceX and Blue Origin, to deliver cargo to the Moon. NASA is also developing a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE, which will explore the Moon’s surface and underground ice. Blue Origin will deliver this rover using their Mark 1 lander. NASA also awarded contracts to companies that will help launch rockets and move supplies between Earth and the Moon.

**Impact** – These projects are important because they create the tools and systems needed for astronauts to live on the Moon safely and for a long time. The PROMISE rover can work during the long lunar night and in dark areas where ice may be found. The new delivery contracts will make sure supplies and equipment arrive on the Moon regularly. This work also uses proven technology from Mars rovers, saving time and money.

**What's next step** – NASA plans to launch the PROMISE rover by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. They will also start building a small power and communication system called miniCAST to support Moon Base activities. Over the next decade, NASA will continue awarding contracts and testing new technology to prepare for astronauts’ arrival and future Mars missions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA is making steady progress toward a lasting human presence on the Moon by developing new robotic explorers, delivery systems, and infrastructure partnerships with commercial companies.

articles.title: A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch
articles.summary: A nuclear explosion might save Earth from a deadly asteroid, but new research suggests that hitting the wrong side could make the difference between success and disaster. Scientists found that an asteroid's irregular shape can dramatically affect how it responds to an X-ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying nearly fivefold depending on the angle.
articles.content:
A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, new research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

A new study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

"We expected aim to matter," said Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much."

The effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how quickly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A New Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

Earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

The new system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

"Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore said. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it."

Why Lumpy Asteroids Change Everything

Moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid."

A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

"You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he said. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid."

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches."

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast

The new computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

The software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

These calculations are important because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

"Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth

Despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research shows that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

"Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully," Moore said. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day."

The new simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

For one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

Nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.

The research provides detailed insights into how asteroid shape affects deflection success, offering practical guidance for future missions. This represents a meaningful advancement in space technology with potential large-scale benefits for humanity's safety.
articles.personality_title: New model shows nuclear blasts must hit the right side of asteroids to protect Earth
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists are studying ways to protect Earth from dangerous asteroids. One idea is to use a nuclear explosion to push an asteroid off course by heating its surface with X-rays. However, real asteroids have bumpy, uneven shapes, which makes it harder to predict how they will move after a blast.

**What happened** – Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories created a new computer model that simulates how nuclear X-ray bursts affect asteroids with realistic shapes. Their study found that the direction of the blast can change the asteroid’s speed by up to five times and its spin by even more. This means aiming at the right side of an asteroid is very important for the blast to work well.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because past models treated asteroids as smooth spheres, which missed how uneven surfaces affect deflection. The new simulation combines two advanced methods to accurately predict how different parts of an asteroid will vaporize and push it in space. This helps scientists plan better ways to stop asteroids without breaking them into dangerous pieces.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to improve the model further to predict if an entire asteroid might break apart after a blast. They also need better 3D images of asteroids and precise ways to deliver nuclear devices in space. This research will guide future missions to choose the best blast location and strength to protect Earth.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new, faster simulation shows that carefully aiming nuclear blasts at the right side of uneven asteroids is key to safely redirecting them away from Earth.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau modèle montre qu'il faut viser le bon côté des astéroïdes avec des explosions nucléaires pour protéger la Terre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent des moyens de protéger la Terre contre les astéroïdes dangereux. Une idée est d'utiliser une explosion nucléaire pour pousser un astéroïde hors de sa trajectoire en chauffant sa surface avec des rayons X. Mais les astéroïdes réels ont des formes irrégulières et bosselées, ce qui complique la prédiction de leur mouvement après une explosion.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs du Laboratoire national Sandia ont créé un nouveau modèle informatique qui simule comment les rafales de rayons X nucléaires affectent des astéroïdes aux formes réalistes. Leur étude montre que la direction de l'explosion peut changer la vitesse de l'astéroïde jusqu'à cinq fois, et sa rotation encore plus. Cela signifie qu'il est très important de viser le bon côté de l'astéroïde pour que l'explosion fonctionne bien.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car les anciens modèles considéraient les astéroïdes comme des sphères lisses, ce qui ne montrait pas comment les surfaces irrégulières influencent la déviation. La nouvelle simulation combine deux méthodes avancées pour prédire avec précision quelles parties de l'astéroïde se vaporisent et comment il est poussé dans l'espace. Cela aide les scientifiques à mieux planifier comment arrêter les astéroïdes sans les casser en morceaux dangereux.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques veulent améliorer le modèle pour prévoir si un astéroïde entier pourrait se briser après une explosion. Ils ont aussi besoin de meilleures images 3D des astéroïdes et de moyens précis pour placer des dispositifs nucléaires dans l'espace. Cette recherche guidera les futures missions pour choisir le meilleur endroit et la bonne puissance d'explosion pour protéger la Terre.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle simulation rapide montre que viser soigneusement le bon côté des astéroïdes irréguliers avec des explosions nucléaires est essentiel pour les dévier en toute sécurité de la Terre.
articles.personality_title_es: Un nuevo modelo muestra que las explosiones nucleares deben impactar el lado correcto de los asteroides para proteger la Tierra
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos buscan formas de proteger la Tierra de asteroides peligrosos. Una idea es usar una explosión nuclear para empujar un asteroide fuera de su camino calentando su superficie con rayos X. Pero los asteroides reales tienen formas irregulares y con bultos, lo que dificulta predecir cómo se moverán después de la explosión.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores del Laboratorio Nacional Sandia crearon un nuevo modelo por computadora que simula cómo los pulsos de rayos X nucleares afectan asteroides con formas reales. Su estudio encontró que la dirección de la explosión puede cambiar la velocidad del asteroide hasta cinco veces y su giro aún más. Esto significa que apuntar al lado correcto del asteroide es muy importante para que la explosión funcione bien.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque los modelos anteriores trataban a los asteroides como esferas lisas, lo que no mostraba cómo las superficies irregulares afectan la desviación. La nueva simulación combina dos métodos avanzados para predecir con precisión qué partes del asteroide se vaporizarán y cómo se empujará en el espacio. Esto ayuda a los científicos a planear mejor cómo detener asteroides sin romperlos en pedazos peligrosos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren mejorar el modelo para predecir si un asteroide entero podría romperse después de la explosión. También necesitan mejores imágenes 3D de asteroides y formas precisas para colocar dispositivos nucleares en el espacio. Esta investigación guiará futuras misiones para elegir el mejor lugar y la fuerza correcta de la explosión para proteger la Tierra.

**Resumen en una frase** – Una nueva simulación rápida muestra que apuntar cuidadosamente al lado correcto de asteroides irregulares con explosiones nucleares es clave para desviarlos de forma segura de la Tierra.

articles.title: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
articles.summary: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground. The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
articles.content:
Mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears. New evidence from mysterious gas emissions near an enormous Martian volcano suggests that heat and volcanic processes could still be present deep beneath the planet's surface.

Researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region. The findings suggest that gases from the planet's interior may be escaping through cracks in the surface, potentially revealing volcanic activity that has remained hidden until now.

An international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground. If confirmed, this would indicate that Mars still has dormant volcanic systems capable of releasing gases to the surface.

The European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in findings reported in 2021. On Earth, hydrogen chloride is frequently released through openings connected to magma, raising the possibility that similar processes could be occurring on Mars.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," says Daniel Mège, Professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the study published in Science Advances.

Mysterious Gas Emissions Defy Mars' Seasonal Pattern

The researchers noticed something unusual during early summer in the Martian northern hemisphere. Hydrogen chloride concentrations were unexpectedly elevated in a particular region, even though the gas normally becomes scarce at that time of year.

Hydrogen chloride levels on Mars generally follow a seasonal cycle. They typically peak during northern winter before declining to very low levels in summer. Scientists believe much of this behavior is associated with the planet's dust and water cycles.

However, the observations revealed a striking exception. Elevated hydrogen chloride repeatedly appeared in early summer over volcanic fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons. The unusual timing and consistent location suggested that something beyond ordinary atmospheric chemistry might be responsible.

Is Mars Still Volcanically Active?

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, but scientists still do not know whether volcanic processes remain active beneath their surfaces.

Images taken from orbit indicate that some Martian volcanoes experienced eruptions within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes, demonstrating that the planet continues to experience seismic activity.

Together, these observations suggest that Mars may retain some of its geological energy. However, scientists have never directly observed a new volcanic eruption or fresh lava flow on the planet, leaving the question of present-day volcanism unresolved.

Fresh Cracks Reveal Clues to Hidden Volcanic Heat

To investigate the unusual gas concentrations, the research team combined atmospheric measurements with detailed observations of the Martian surface.

The Atmospheric Chemistry Suite aboard TGO uses infrared spectrometers to identify gases in the atmosphere. These instruments detected hydrogen chloride concentrated in a relatively small area shortly after the disappearance of winter frost.

Researchers then examined the same region using the orbiter's CaSSIS camera. The images revealed narrow fractures that appeared relatively fresh, with some extending hundreds of meters across the surface. Unusual changes in surface color were also visible around the cracks.

"The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," explains Daniel.

One possible explanation is that gases originating from magma deep underground travel upward through these fractures. On Earth, comparable volcanic openings are known as fumaroles.

The researchers propose that extremely cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to -120°C, allow ice to seal the fractures and temporarily prevent gases from escaping. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice sublimates, changing directly into vapor and potentially opening pathways for underground gases to reach the atmosphere.

The discoloration observed around the fractures could also be significant. It may result from minerals or other substances deposited by escaping gases, similar to the deposits commonly found around fumaroles (volcanic gas vents) on Earth.

A Possible Magma Chamber Beneath Mars

Although the connection between the gas emissions and volcanic fractures appeared promising, the researchers needed to rule out other explanations.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," concedes Daniel.

The team carefully evaluated the chemical reactions that could produce hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere, including processes unrelated to volcanism.

"A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food," adds Daniel.

After examining the atmospheric and geological evidence together, the researchers proposed that the gas could be escaping from a dormant magma chamber beneath Alba Mons. Such a chamber would form part of an underground volcanic system that could continue releasing gases even without producing visible eruptions.

Hidden Volcanic Activity Could Help Mars Support Life

The implications may extend beyond understanding the planet's geological history. Volcanic gases could also provide clues about how Mars evolved and whether it ever supported environments suitable for life.

In the distant past, gases released from magma, including hydrogen chloride, may have helped create a denser atmosphere and warmer conditions. Those conditions could have allowed liquid water to remain across large portions of the Martian surface.

Volcanic activity might also create habitable environments underground. If rising magma or lava comes into contact with groundwater, the interaction can produce warm hydrothermal systems. Such environments could provide both chemical energy and protection from the harsh conditions on the surface.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," ponders Daniel.

Although the findings do not establish that Mars is currently erupting or that life exists beneath its surface, they offer an intriguing new reason to investigate the volcanic fractures around Alba Mons.

"These findings may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet," highlights Colin Wilson, ESA's project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

articles.personality_title: New gas leaks hint Mars may still have underground volcanic activity
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wondered if Mars is geologically dead or if it still has some volcanic activity beneath its surface. Mars has the largest volcanoes in the solar system, but no recent eruptions have been seen.

**What happened** – Researchers studying gases above a large Martian volcano called Alba Mons found unusual amounts of hydrogen chloride gas. This gas often comes from hot magma on Earth. Using instruments on the European Space Agency’s ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, they spotted this gas near fresh cracks on the volcano’s slopes during early summer when it usually disappears.

**Impact** – These findings suggest Mars might still have heat and volcanic processes underground. The gas could be escaping through cracks sealed by ice in winter and opening in warmer months. This means there could be pockets of warmth and chemical energy below the surface, which might support microbial life. It also shows Mars may be more active than thought.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue observing these gas leaks and volcanic cracks to confirm if magma is still moving underground. Future missions might explore these areas directly to learn more about Mars’s volcanic activity and search for signs of life.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Unusual gas leaks near fresh cracks on Mars reveal the planet may still have underground volcanic activity, opening new possibilities for its geology and habitability.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps si Mars est géologiquement morte ou si elle a encore une activité volcanique sous sa surface. Mars possède les plus grands volcans du système solaire, mais aucune éruption récente n’a été observée.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont trouvé des quantités inhabituelles de gaz chlorure d’hydrogène au-dessus d’un grand volcan martien appelé Alba Mons. Sur Terre, ce gaz vient souvent du magma chaud. Grâce à des instruments de l’orbiteur ExoMars de l’Agence spatiale européenne, ils ont détecté ce gaz près de fissures fraîches sur les pentes du volcan au début de l’été, alors qu’il disparaît normalement.

**Impact** – Ces découvertes suggèrent que Mars pourrait encore avoir de la chaleur et des processus volcaniques sous terre. Le gaz pourrait s’échapper par des fissures scellées par la glace en hiver et s’ouvrir en saison chaude. Cela signifie qu’il pourrait y avoir des poches de chaleur et d’énergie chimique sous la surface, capables de soutenir la vie microbienne. Cela montre aussi que Mars est peut-être plus active que ce que l’on croyait.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à observer ces fuites de gaz et fissures volcaniques pour confirmer si du magma bouge encore sous terre. Les prochaines missions pourraient explorer directement ces zones pour mieux comprendre l’activité volcanique martienne et chercher des signes de vie.

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas fugas de gas sugieren que Marte podría tener actividad volcánica subterránea
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos se han preguntado si Marte está geológicamente muerto o si aún tiene actividad volcánica bajo su superficie. Marte tiene los volcanes más grandes del sistema solar, pero no se han visto erupciones recientes.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores encontraron cantidades inusuales de gas cloruro de hidrógeno sobre un gran volcán marciano llamado Alba Mons. En la Tierra, este gas suele provenir del magma caliente. Usando instrumentos del orbitador ExoMars de la Agencia Espacial Europea, detectaron este gas cerca de grietas frescas en las laderas del volcán durante el verano temprano, cuando normalmente desaparece.

**Impacto** – Estos hallazgos sugieren que Marte podría aún tener calor y procesos volcánicos bajo tierra. El gas podría escapar por grietas selladas por hielo en invierno y abrirse en meses cálidos. Esto indica que podrían existir bolsillos de calor y energía química bajo la superficie que podrían apoyar vida microbiana. También muestra que Marte podría estar más activo de lo que se pensaba.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán observando estas fugas de gas y grietas volcánicas para confirmar si el magma aún se mueve bajo tierra. Misiones futuras podrían explorar estas áreas directamente para aprender más sobre la actividad volcánica de Marte y buscar señales de vida.

**Resumen en una frase** – Fugas inusuales de gas cerca de grietas frescas en Marte revelan que el planeta podría tener actividad volcánica subterránea, abriendo nuevas posibilidades para su geología y habitabilidad.
